reading.rtitle: Waiting Rooms -- an artist statement, and an editor reading it
paras: Statement. My practice is an ongoing investigation of the waiting room as a site of care. Through the accumulation of small objects left behind by patients, and the documentation of the hours they spend there, the work interrogates the institutional organization of time. Its materiality is deliberate: the paper, the plastic chairs and the fluorescent light are the same ones the clinic uses. The installation foregrounds the absence of the patient rather than the presence of the doctor, and situates this preoccupation within a longer conversation about who is allowed to be seen.

Read it again and count the verbs that are doing any work. There are almost none. Investigation, accumulation, documentation, organization, absence, presence: six nouns, each of them a verb or an adjective that has been frozen. This is nominalization, and it is how academic and institutional English sounds. It is not wrong. It lets a writer hold a whole process in one word and then say something about it, which is why a jury expects to see some of it. The problem is that it also hides who is doing what. Who collects the objects? Who records the hours? In the statement above, nobody does, and the artist disappears from her own work.

Editors who work with artists on these texts tend to give the same advice. Keep a nominalization where it is precise and there is no shorter way to say it: materiality, for example, has no plain equivalent. Unpack it where it is only jargon, so that the documentation of the hours becomes I record how long each patient waits. A statement a jury can read in ninety seconds usually has one abstract noun per sentence, not four, and at least one sentence in which the artist is the subject of an active verb. A legible statement is not a simpler one. It is one in which the reader can always tell what is at stake.

listenings.text: Every spring I read about four hundred artist statements for one open call, and I can tell you exactly what happens in the first thirty seconds. I look for a sentence in which the artist does something. Not the practice, not the work, not the investigation. The artist. I record, I collect, I interview. If I reach the end of the first paragraph and I still cannot say what this person physically does in the studio, I move on. I am not proud of it, but that is the reality of a jury with four hundred files. The second thing I look for is one idea I have not already read that morning. Everybody interrogates something. Everybody foregrounds something. Those words have been used so often that they have stopped carrying anything. The statements that stay with me are usually the plainest ones, written by people who clearly know the theory and decided not to show off with it.

Most of the artists who come to me have already written the statement, and it is almost always too abstract, not too simple. So the first thing we do together is find the nouns that are hiding verbs. Documentation, representation, investigation. For each one I ask a very plain question: who does it, and to what? The answer usually goes straight into the new version, as a sentence with the artist as the subject. Then we keep the two or three abstract nouns that are genuinely doing work, the ones with no shorter way to say them. Materiality is often one of those. Finally, I ask the artist to read the whole thing aloud to somebody outside the art world. If that person can repeat back what is at stake in one sentence, the statement is finished. If they cannot, we distill it again. It usually takes three rounds, and it is always the third version that gets sent.
